name: Nutrafol
lead: Nutrafol is a branded oral supplement taken as capsules to support thicker-looking, fuller hair. People who notice thinning at the part line, the temples or the crown use it as a daily, non-prescription addition to a hair routine, either on its own or alongside treatments such as minoxidil or finasteride. The chain is straightforward: the botanical and nutrient blend is intended to act on factors linked to shedding and thinning (stress, inflammation, DHT), which the product's trial papers report as more hairs per area and better hair quality, which in turn reads as more density.[1][2]

Its published trials describe a proprietary Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals said to have anti-inflammatory, adaptogenic, antioxidant and dihydrotestosterone-inhibiting properties.[1] Several small randomised and open-label studies of Nutrafol formulations in women, menopausal women, women on plant-based diets and mixed groups have reported increases in hair counts or improved self-assessment.[1][2][3][4]

A 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review of nutritional supplements for hair loss in people without a known deficiency listed Nutrafol among the interventions with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit, while cautioning that its findings should be interpreted carefully.[5] Nutrafol has also been included in network meta-analyses that compared it with drugs, lasers and other supplements.[13][15] It is sold as a dietary supplement, not an approved drug.

paras: Nutrafol is marketed as a once-daily capsule regimen built around a multi-ingredient botanical blend. The company's trial publications describe the blend, called the Synergen Complex, as combining standardized plant extracts chosen to address several drivers of thinning at once, rather than a single pathway.[1] The product line has been split into versions for women, women in perimenopause and menopause, men, and people following plant-based diets, and the trial literature mirrors that split.[1][2][3][4][6]

Reviews of oral supplements for androgenetic alopecia describe Nutrafol and Viviscal as the two most-studied branded nutraceuticals, and note that such products generally face less rigorous testing requirements than pharmaceuticals.[6]

The trial papers say the botanical blend targets stress, inflammation, oxidative stress and DHT, the androgen metabolite linked to follicle miniaturisation in androgenetic alopecia.[1] For menopausal women the formulation is described as addressing hormonal transition as one contributor to thinning.[2] The vegan-formulation paper frames diet and nutrition as part of a multi-factorial cause of thinning and says women on plant-based diets have particular nutrient needs.[3]
These mechanistic statements come from the product's own publications; the studies measured hair counts and ratings rather than demonstrating each pathway directly.

A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of Nutrafol Women's Capsules in women with self-perceived thinning (26 active, 14 placebo) reported significantly more terminal and vellus hairs on phototrichogram at days 90 and 180 than placebo, improved investigator-rated hair growth and quality, and no reported adverse events.[1]

A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in perimenopausal, menopausal and postmenopausal women (40 active, 30 placebo) reported increases in terminal and total hair counts versus placebo, a 32.41 percent reduction in shedding by day 180, and good tolerability.[2]

A prospective single-blind six-month study enrolled 47 men aged 20 to 55 and 51 premenopausal women aged 20 to 45 with self-perceived mild-to-moderate thinning, across African American, Asian, Hispanic Caucasian and Non-Hispanic Caucasian groups, and assessed perceived hair growth and quality.[4] A multicentre study of the vegan formulation in women following plant-based diets and a 2026 multi-arm six-month study of hair fibre thickness and strength add further data.[3][7]

Registered trials include a small study in women with thinning hair (21 participants), a placebo-controlled study in women (40), a peri/menopausal study (70), a vegan-botanical study in women (110), and a study in males (112); two further trials started in 2024 enrolled 250 and 181 participants.[8][9][10][20][11][16][17]

A 2022 review of nutraceuticals for androgenetic alopecia concluded that Nutrafol and Viviscal were effective to a modest degree in men and women and could serve as adjuncts to current treatments.[6] A Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials of at least 20 patients and 24 weeks listed Nutrafol alongside minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride, low-level laser and other options when comparing terminal-hair regrowth by sex.[13] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies and 967 participants on commercial oral supplements, which included Nutrafol among Ceramosides, Viviscal, Nourkrin and others, reported significant improvements versus placebo on measures such as telogen hair density.[15] A 2025 network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia noted that the field is limited by small samples and a lack of head-to-head comparisons.[12]

Most Nutrafol trials are small, last about six months and use the manufacturer's own proprietary products; the 2023 JAMA Dermatology review described the overall nutritional-supplement literature as needing cautious interpretation.[5]

Trials report no or few adverse events.[1][2] The JAMA Dermatology review found adverse effects to be rare and mild across the supplements evaluated.[5] A 2026 disproportionality analysis examined dietary supplement adverse events in the FDA CAERS database generally.[14]

On T Nation, members discussing shedding mention Nutrafol as one item in a stack; one poster describes using Nizoral 1%, Nutrafol and MK-677 together while trying to stop shedding, and another lists Nutrafol alongside ketoconazole, finasteride, minoxidil and dutasteride while asking about hair support during a steroid course.[18][19] These posts are personal accounts and do not report controlled results.

lore.intro: Forum members tend to describe Nutrafol as a supplement added to a broader hair-retention routine rather than a replacement for drugs.[18][19]

claims.claim: Nutrafol supports hair retention as an add-on to other hair treatments.
claims.believers: Posters on T Nation list it alongside ketoconazole shampoo, finasteride, minoxidil and dutasteride when trying to slow shedding.[18][19]
claims.experts: A 2022 review found modest hair-growth effects for Nutrafol and Viviscal and described them as possible adjuncts to existing treatments.[6]

claims.believers: The product's trial papers describe dihydrotestosterone-inhibiting properties of its Synergen Complex.[1]
claims.experts: The trials measured hair counts and ratings; they are small and short, and a JAMA Dermatology review asked for cautious interpretation of supplement studies.[5]

card.summary: Branded botanical hair supplement with several small positive trials, mostly in women, and a cautiously rated evidence base.
card.note: Dietary supplement, not a DHT-blocking drug; trials are small and short.

quick.overview:
Nutrafol is a branded capsule of plant extracts and nutrients sold for thinning hair. Several small, mostly six-month studies in women, menopausal women and some men report more hairs per area than placebo or baseline.

A 2023 systematic review included it among supplements with the highest-quality evidence of possible benefit, with the caution that the research base is limited.
quick.mechanism: The product's papers say its Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals targets stress hormones, inflammation, oxidative stress and DHT. Those mechanisms have not been shown in large independent trials.
quick.risks: Trials report few or no adverse events, and a systematic review called supplement side effects rare and mild. It is sold as a dietary supplement, not an approved drug.
